result:
The premise isn't right: more agents don't always give better results. So the answer is neither five nor ten. Start with one.

Take a real request: "Is the laser cutter free Thursday at 3, and what safety training do I need?" One agent with three tools handles it in one loop. It calls the calendar tool, searches the manual, and writes the answer.

Now split it into five agents: a router, a manual agent, a calendar agent, a booking agent and a summarizer. Every handoff means a new model call that has to be given the context again. Each call costs tokens. Details also get lost between agents, and any one agent can get it wrong. Your budget is small, so this hurts. Anthropic's engineering write-up on its multi-agent research system says these setups use several times more tokens than a single agent. I'm quoting that from memory, so check the number before you use it at your design review.

Splitting pays off in a few cases:
- The subtasks are independent and can run in parallel.
- One agent's context would get too big to hold everything.
- One agent has so many tools that it picks the wrong one.

Your assistant has three tools, short tasks, and mostly one step after another, so none of these apply yet. Booking is a good candidate for a fixed workflow. Check availability, confirm with the student, then book. That sequence doesn't need a model to decide the order.

My recommendation: build one agent with three tools. Measure its cost and its mistakes. Split only when you can point to a specific failure that a split would fix. That gives you a reason to defend at the review.

Quick check: which of the three splitting cases is closest to your assistant's manuals, and why? I can write a lesson on when multi-agent systems pay off if you'd like one.
